catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-1-q1.explanation: C - capture To capture a moment is a paraphrase of “to take a picture, to photograph”. To seize the moment means “to enjoy yourself now rather that later”. Other two variants do not collocate.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-1-q2.explanation: B - rightRight in front of is the only existing collocation of the four given here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-1-q3.explanation: C - counting To count on something or somebody means “to rely on it, to put trust in it”. To settle on something means “to decide or choose something”, but the previous sentence states that people do it “mindlessly”, so no actual choice is made. The remaining two options do not fit.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-1-q4.explanation: C - attendTo attend to something means “to try and deal with something”. Pay attention to the preposition “to”. Engage in is a common use for the first verb. Dedicate somebody to something fits here, but “dedicate” and “somebody” can’t be separated. Apply to isn’t used for the same reason.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-1-q5.explanation: D - impactTo have a negative impact on something is a widely used collocation. A common mistake is to choose “result”. It is rarely used with the “on” preposition, so impactis a better choice here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-1-q6.explanation: C - ledThe students were led on a tour (past participle of lead), which means that someone was leading them, and it is explained right after that they were asked to do something. The other three variants do not convey this message.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-1-q7.explanation: A - accurateAll four variants collocate well with the preposition; however, only the first adjective fits. Accurate here means “correct, precise” which are the words we need, judging by context.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-1-q8.explanation: B - compared We compare how likely people are to remember things they have seen and those they have photographed.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-2-q9.explanation: It here refers to the New Generation Award. Note that “which” and “that” should be used here as the sentence uses “it” which acts as the subject of the sentence.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-2-q10.explanation: whose The context suggests that the mentioned start-up belongs to Kathryn Parsons.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-2-q11.explanation: be To overestimate something is to give it more importance than it deserves. In this case, the importance is justified as it creates role models for women.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-2-q12.explanation: “That they can do it, too” is the part that helps us choose the right pronoun. It should be “them”, and not “everyone” or “everybody”.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-2-q13.explanation: “Between” works great here. “Among” is more commonly used when there is no clear definition of range

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-2-q15.explanation: with/havingThe question here is, “what kind of women do they want to recognize?”. Women with or women having a mission and a vision.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-2-q16.explanation: To make the world a better place is a widely used set phrase.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-3-q17.explanation: annoyance This is the only noun that can be formed from annoy.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-3-q18.explanation: bearing Remember that you can’t use the same word form as the one given in the task.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-3-q19.explanation: reference Indefinite article “a” suggests that we need to make it a noun.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-3-q20.explanation: emotional Angry or ____ means that the second word has to be an adjective too.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-3-q22.explanation: offence Again, a noun should be used. Don’t forget that offense is the AmE spelling and therefore shouldn’t be used here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-3-q23.explanation: disclose To disclose means “to reveal, to make known”.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-3-q24.explanation: truthful An adjective is required here. Mind your spelling, there should be only one letter

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-4-q25.explanation: there is/was hardly any petrol Almost no = hardly any.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-4-q26.explanation: had no idea (that) cars cost Had no idea = didn’t know

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-4-q27.explanation: let it get you To be depressed = to be down. The second sentence is in the passive voice, so to make someone depressed = to get someone down.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-4-q28.explanation: to be making a recovery We still have to use a continuous tense here, so we use “making” with recovery. Remember that the given word can’t be changed.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-4-q29.answer: take her work seriously enough according
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-4-q29.explanation: take her work seriously enough according To have a serious attitude to something = to take it seriously.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-4-q30.answer: causing you such a lot of
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-4-q30.explanation: causing you such a lot of Confuse so much – cause a lot of confusion.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-5-q31.explanation: D A, B and C can all be used as the answer, but it will be incomplete. Answer D summarises the idea of the paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-5-q32.explanation: BThe second sentence of this paragraph holds the answer — how drastically the modern British homes got transformed. Answer D is mentioned, however, it is not the key topic of this paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-5-q33.explanation: A This paragraph is about “decentralisation” of an average British home, how the living room is no longer the main place in it, and therefore people no longer spend most of their time there. Answers B and D are mentioned, but only as supporting ideas.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-5-q34.explanation: D Answers B and C do not fit — there is no mentioning about advertising or functionality of the inventions. Answer A can’t be used because of the way it states that most inventions were dangerous, which isn’t true.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-5-q35.explanation: B Quoting the exact excerpt: “it would be impossible for anyone to imagine their front room as a “parlour” without seeming deeply old-fashioned”

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-5-q36.explanation: C The following sentence has a M. Thatcher example that shows how little home life in Britain have changed.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-6-q37.explanation: C Reviewer C believes that the companies chosen for the show are very unique and therefore are not a good representation of the industry. All other reviewers hold that the companies in the show are well-chosen to give a good idea of how the industry functions.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-6-q38.explanation: ABoth A and B talk about the probability of viewers losing interest as the content of this show might be too difficult to understand at first.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-6-q39.explanation: C Reviewer C is the only one who thinks that the people in charge are portrayed as not having too many responsibilities, always able to delegate their tasks to subordinates. All other reviewers state that higher-ups are shows as hard-working, decision-making individuals.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-6-q40.explanation: A Both A and C believe that the interview questions were not comprehensive enough.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-7-q41.explanation: G To understand this paragraph, it is important to know that sailors refer to their ships as if they were women; therefore, the pronoun “she” used by the captain refers to the freighter vessel. This is later confirmed in the next paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-7-q42.explanation: C Beginning the paragraph, the author talks about how he came to like the ship despite its unappealing look. The second part of the paragraph focuses on the uneasy situation that made the author like the ship.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-7-q43.explanation: E“Hoping so” is a clear reference to the last part of the previous paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-7-q44.explanation: FThe beginning of next paragraph uses pronoun “they” to refer to the waves, mentioned at the end of this paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-7-q45.explanation: B“That condition” is clearly described in the previous paragraph. The beginning of the next paragraph states that “all was well in that regard”, referring to the food supply that the electrician checked.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-7-q46.explanation: DThe paragraph names what were inside the container mentioned in the previous paragraph. The beginning of the next paragraph refers to the sailors who make sea navigation possible.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-8-q47.explanation: ESign representing “20” has become simpler, formerly needing two hands to show and later only one hand.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-8-q48.explanation: BMiddle of the paragraph compares how hearing and deaf individuals mime a story about a cat walking down the street.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-8-q49.explanation: BBelow the middle of the paragraph. Similar signs in combinations can have different meanings.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-8-q50.explanation: CThe process of language evolution with pidgin language taken as an example

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-8-q51.explanation: DFirst sentence of the paragraph talks about a specialised part of the human brain.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-8-q52.explanation: D Last sentence of the same paragraph. Children’s minds are “primed” to learn the rules of grammar — meaning that it is much easier to learn them when young.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-8-q53.explanation: EFirst sentence — the visits have been taking place every year since 1990.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-8-q54.explanation: AThe second part of the paragraph mentions how older generations of children passed on their knowledge to the younger ones.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-8-q55.explanation: EThe last sentence of the paragraph states that the children want a sign for a particular reason, in this case — one that can be shown quickly.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test2-part-8-q56.explanation: DThe first sentence of the paragraph has two opposing ideas on the language origin.
